rows.selection_reason: Existing evidence is nonexistent, so the first experiment should establish a baseline for multimodal performance. This tests the simplest multimodal configuration (singleprofile, pca_n2000 RNA encoder, resnet50 image encoder) with basic concatenation fusion. It clarifies whether multimodal approaches outperform single-modality baselines and isolates the effect of fusion method.

The existing evidence shows that config_016 (multimodal) achieves 0.5266 validation accuracy. This experiment tests a unimodal RNA-only model using the same pca_n2000 encoder as config_016, isolating the impact of adding image data. It directly addresses whether multimodal approaches provide performance benefits over unimodal RNA-only models, a critical design decision with high uncertainty.

Existing evidence shows multimodal models (config_016: 0.5266 accuracy) outperform rna_only (config_001: 0.4849). This experiment tests weighted fusion vs. concat fusion in the same multimodal setup (same encoders, profile setting, aggregation), isolating the impact of fusion method. It balances exploitation (building on multimodal success) and exploration (testing critical design choice).

Existing evidence shows multimodal singleprofile models (config_016: 0.526 accuracy) outperform RNA-only (config_001: 0.484). This experiment tests multiprofile with avgpool aggregation (untested in multimodal) to isolate the impact of profile setting and aggregation. It directly compares to config_016 (singleprofile, no aggregation) while keeping RNA/image encoders consistent, addressing key uncertainties about multiprofile benefits and aggregation methods.

Existing evidence shows that multimodal models with multiprofile settings (config_018: 0.6186 accuracy) outperform singleprofile and rna_only models. This experiment tests whether changing the fusion method from concat to weighted (while keeping other parameters identical) improves performance. It isolates the effect of fusion strategy, a critical design choice, and builds on the strong baseline of config_018. This is the best use of the next experiment as it directly addresses uncertainty about fusion methods' impact on accuracy.

Existing evidence shows that multimodal multiprofile models with avgpool aggregation and weighted fusion (config_019) achieve the highest accuracy so far (0.639). This experiment tests replacing avgpool with transformer aggregation while keeping RNA encoder, image encoder, and fusion method consistent. This isolates the effect of aggregation method, a key design choice, and could reveal if transformer aggregation improves performance. It balances exploitation (building on a proven setup) and exploration (testing a new component).

The existing evidence shows that multimodal models with multiprofile, avgpool aggregation, and weighted fusion (e.g., config_019) achieve the highest validation accuracy (0.639). This experiment tests whether replacing the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l (a more complex model) further improves performance, isolating the effect of the image encoder while keeping other critical parameters (multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion) consistent. This is a high-impact comparison that could either validate the benefit of advanced image encoders or refine the understanding of optimal component choices.

Existing evidence shows that multimodal models with multiprofile, weighted fusion, and avgpool aggregation (e.g., config_019, config_025) achieve high validation accuracy. This experiment tests whether switching the RNA encoder from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200 (a more complex encoder) while keeping other components (image encoder: imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted fusion) the same would improve performance. This isolates the impact of RNA encoder choice, a critical design decision with uncertain optimal trade-offs between complexity and effectiveness.

Existing evidence shows that using scvi_n200 RNA encoder, imagenet_vit_l image encoder, multiprofile, and weighted fusion (config_037) achieves high accuracy. This experiment tests whether changing the aggregation method from avgpool to transformer (while keeping fusion as weighted) improves performance, isolating the impact of aggregation. This addresses a key design choice with minimal changes, leveraging prior success while exploring a critical component.

Existing evidence shows that using transformer aggregation with weighted fusion (config_039) achieves high accuracy (0.725). This experiment tests the effect of changing fusion type from weighted to concat while keeping other parameters (scvi_n200 RNA, imagenet_vit_l image, transformer aggregation) consistent. It isolates the impact of fusion strategy, a critical design choice, without altering multiple factors simultaneously.
